growth_story.headline: Cambodia's peace-era boom, built on garments, tourism and a credit-fed building surge, has slowed since 2018 as property cooled and new shocks piled up.
growth_story.arc: In the data, income per person in the 1990–1998 era averages -4.7 percent a year, but nearly all of that comes from one year, 1994, at -39.2. From 1999 to 2007 growth averaged 8.4 percent a year as peace and security returned after decades of conflict, aid and private money flowed in, and the economy opened up, with garment exports and tourism leading; income per person rose from 499 in 1998 to 1,030 in 2007. Growth eased to 5.5 percent a year over 2008–2017, after a dip to 2.4 in 2009 when Western demand for garments and tourism fell, while a long credit boom tied to construction and property ran through that decade. Since 2018 growth has averaged 3.4 percent a year: the pandemic cut income per person by 5.0 percent in 2020, and the recovery has been held back by a property slump, the end of the credit boom, the 2025 border conflict with Thailand and higher fuel prices in 2026. Even so, income per person reached a new high of 2,273 in 2025, and growth over 2016–2025 averaged 4.0 percent a year against 6.0 in the decade before.

threads.title: Peace opens the door
threads.text: Growth took off once peace and security returned in the late 1990s, after decades of conflict. Large public and private capital inflows and an open economy followed, and income per person roughly doubled between 1998 and 2007.

threads.title: A narrow base of garments and tourism
threads.text: Growth rested on a few sectors: garment exports and tourism, then construction and property. Because garments and tourism sell mostly to Western buyers, the 2009 world recession hit hard, and growth in income per person fell to 2.4 percent that year.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe growth as rapid from the early 1990s, once the national accounts were rebuilt. The data instead show the 1990–1998 era averaging -4.7 percent a year. That average rests almost entirely on one year, 1994, when income per person drops 39.2 percent, from 845 to 514. The sources describe no fall of that size; the setbacks they name for the 1990s are the July 1997 political fighting and the 1997–1998 Asian crisis. So the era's average says more about how the data series was built than about events the sources describe.
